props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · scripted sweep of flip
props.title: A Table That Moves Points

B01.capture_spec: C01: 08-flip.gdshader on a Sprite2D; card texture drawn at 1024 px (U = 8 times the 128 px card; a clean cream card, warm grey border, teal arrow pointing right, small teal square top left), node scale k/8 with k = 2.0 in a 1280x720 logical canvas, every pixel-valued uniform multiplied by U; 4K SubViewport route, Forward+, 30 fps, offline fixed tick, no input; 17 s. flip keyframes (fraction of the beat, ease in-out on each move): 0.0 at 0.00 to 0.10, 0.5 at 0.38, 0.5 until 0.62, 1.0 at 0.80, 1.0 to the end. At the 50 % mark: the mirrored back, fully visible (arrow points left). At 85 %: the front. Verified: widths 128 x |cos(TAU x flip)|, mirrored at 0.5 (geometry-summary.txt).
B01.visual_intent: Act title 'A Table That Moves Points' (serif 40) top-left. A real Godot render in a framed window on the cream stage: a cream card with a teal arrow pointing right and a small teal square in its top left corner sits still, then turns over like a card: it narrows to an edge, comes back mirrored (the arrow now points left, the square sits top right), then turns back to the front. Label under the window: 'scripted sweep'.
B01.motion_claim: The flat card turns over, narrows to nothing, comes back mirrored, and turns to the front again.

show.event: back side: the arrow points left

B01.runner_up: manim drawing of a card turning
B01.why: A real render is the honest picture of 'a flat picture that turns over'; a drawing would only claim it.

B02.visual_intent: Left to right on the cream stage: a bracketed two-by-two table (1 3 over 2 4) labelled 'table', a bracketed column (5 over 6) labelled 'point', an equals sign and an empty bracketed result column. A terracotta ring outlines the table's top row (labelled 'row'); the small products '1 x 5' and '3 x 6' appear beneath and add up to '23', which lands in the first result slot. The ring drops to the bottom row: '2 x 5' and '4 x 6' add up to '34'. Last, a drawn arrow runs from the point column to the result column.
B02.motion_claim: A ring walks down the table one row at a time, and each row collapses into one number of the answer.

show.event: table, point, equals sign, empty result
ring on the top row; products 1 x 5 and 3 x 6
ring drops to the bottom row; products 2 x 5 and 4 x 6
arrow from the point to the result

B02.runner_up: Remotion card with the arithmetic typed out
B02.why: A ring that walks down the rows shows 'row against point' as an action; typed arithmetic would only list it.

cues.label: mat2: a table of four numbers

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · shader switched on at 60 % of the beat

B03.capture_spec: C02: a ColorRect filling the result window; no material for the first 60 % of the beat, then 01-table-check.gdshader assigned (harness option --material-at); 11 s; 4K SubViewport route, Forward+, 30 fps, offline fixed tick, no input. At the 50 % mark: the plain stage colour (shader not yet on) with line 5 in focus. At 85 %: teal. Verified: probe (0.3686, 0.6392, 0.5686); the disagree colour is (0.85, 0.2, 0.2).
B03.visual_intent: Code card at left with the real ten-line shader; at right a framed Godot window that is the plain stage colour at first, then turns teal when the check line is highlighted. A small readout 'teal: agrees' lands under the window.
B03.motion_claim: Focus steps from the table line to the multiplication to the check, and then the window turns teal.

show.event: check lines; window turns teal; readout lands

B03.why: The claim is 'the shader agrees with my hand calculation'; code beside a result that changes colour on the check line shows it, a bare code card does not.

B04.visual_intent: On the left a code card (Menlo, at least 32) holds the real line mat2(vec2(1.0, 2.0), vec2(3.0, 4.0)); the two vec2 groups are outlined, one solid and one dashed. On the right an empty bracketed two-by-two table. The first vec2 (1, 2) lifts out of the code and stands upright as the table's left column, labelled 'column'; the second (3, 4) becomes the right column. Then the top row is outlined and labelled 'row: 1, 3'.
B04.motion_claim: Each vec2 lifts out of the code and stands upright as a column of the table.

show.event: code line with its two vec2 groups outlined
(1, 2) stands up as the left column; label 'column'
(3, 4) stands up as the right column

B04.why: The surprise is that the order in the code and the order on paper differ; only a drawing that moves the numbers from one to the other shows it.

props.caption: Godot 4.7 documentation · Shading language · captured at build time

B05.visual_intent: The real Godot 4.7 shading-language page in a browser window, scrolled to the 'Constructing' section; the camera pushes in on the sentence that says matrix types are built from vectors 'interpreted as columns' and one terracotta ring marks it.
B05.motion_claim: The camera pushes in on the sentence the voice is quoting.

show.event: push-in; ring on the 'interpreted as columns' sentence

B05.why: The claim is a documentation claim; the documentation itself is the evidence (SHOW-THE-THING).

B06.visual_intent: Three stacked lines on the cream stage. Top (ink): the right reading, table x point = (23, 34). Middle (grey, with a terracotta strike line): the numbers read as ROWS, so the table becomes 1 2 over 3 4 (the 2 and the 3 swap places) and the result is (17, 39); label 'rows'. Bottom (grey, with a strike line): the point written on the LEFT of the table, (5, 6) x table, result (17, 39); the code label 'p * table' beside it. At the end the top line is ringed and a label 'table first' lands.
B06.motion_claim: The 2 and the 3 swap places, and the answer changes to (17, 39); then the point hops to the other side of the table and gives the same wrong answer.

show.event: point jumps to the left of the table; result (17, 39); strike

B06.why: A swap of two numbers and a hop of the point are motions; a table of wrong answers would hide how little it takes to get them.

B07.visual_intent: A grid in Godot's screen directions (x to the right, y DOWN; small axis labels). The unit square with an 'across' arrow (solid) and a 'down' arrow (dashed). At the top right the table 1 3 over 2 4 with its first column outlined solid and its second dashed. The grid warps: the across arrow lands at (1, 2), the down arrow at (3, 4), the square becomes a parallelogram with corners (0,0), (1,2), (4,6), (3,4); tip labels '1, 2' and '3, 4'. Then the view zooms out and a staircase of five across-steps then six down-steps walks from the origin to a terracotta dot labelled '23, 34'.
B07.motion_claim: The square warps into a parallelogram on the two columns, then a staircase of five and six steps walks to (23, 34).

show.event: grid, unit square, two arrows, table with outlined columns
grid warps; arrows land on (1, 2) and (3, 4)
five across-steps then six down-steps walk out

B07.why: The idea is a transformation of a whole grid; only a warping grid shows 'where the arrows land' at a glance.

B08.visual_intent: The warped grid of the previous picture on the same screen-direction axes, with the table 1 3 over 2 4. The four entries change to 1 0 over 0 1 and the grid relaxes back into the plain unit square while both arrows spring back onto (1, 0) and (0, 1). A label 'identity: moves nothing'. A small code card then shows mat2(1.0).
B08.motion_claim: The warped grid relaxes back into a square as the numbers settle to one, zero, zero, one.

show.event: label 'identity: moves nothing'; code card mat2(1.0)

B08.why: 'Moves nothing' is the grid coming to rest; the same table numbers changing live make the point that the numbers ARE the move.

B09.visual_intent: The same screen-direction grid. The table 1 0 over 0 1 becomes 2 0 over 0 2; both arrows stretch to (2, 0) and (0, 2) and the unit square grows into a square twice as wide and tall, centred on the origin's corner. A label 'scale: twice as far' defines the word.
B09.motion_claim: Both arrows stretch to twice their length and the square grows with them.

show.event: entries become 2 0 / 0 2; arrows stretch; square doubles

B09.why: Scaling is a stretch of the arrows; seeing the arrows grow as the diagonal numbers change is the claim.

B10.visual_intent: The test rectangle (a wide rectangle, 3 by 2 grid units, centred on the origin of the screen-direction grid) with four terracotta corner dots; the table 2 0 over 0 2 at the side. The four dots fly outward one after another to their doubled positions and the rectangle's edges redraw between them; a faint ghost of the old rectangle stays. A label 'one table, four corners'.
B10.motion_claim: Four dots fly outward one after another and the rectangle's edges follow them.

show.event: dot 1 flies to its new place

B10.why: The cast of the whole film is the rectangle with four corner dots; dots flying to their new places is the literal meaning of 'multiply every corner'.
